figures.caption: Signed velocity gives displacement. Total distance requires adding the absolute changes.

figures.label: fig:antiderivative-family-shifts
figures.caption: Antiderivatives of the same function differ by vertical shifts. Their slopes at the same \(x\)-value are equal.

figures.label: fig:oriented-interval
figures.caption: The same interval with opposite orientations gives integrals with opposite signs.

figures.label: fig:substitution-stretching-scale
figures.caption: The substitution \(x=u^2\) stretches the measuring scale. Equal \(u\)-steps do not give equal \(x\)-steps.

figures.label: fig:warning-jump-accumulation
figures.caption: A jump discontinuity in \(f\) can produce a corner in the accumulation function \(A\).

figures.label: fig:signed-area-cancellation-line
figures.caption: The integral of \(x\) from \(-1\) to \(1\) is zero because positive and negative signed areas cancel.

figures.label: fig:chapter9-ftc-map
figures.caption: The Fundamental Theorem connects rate, accumulation, antiderivative, and net change.

figures.label: fig:reconstruct-from-rate-data
figures.caption: To reconstruct \(Q(t)\), accumulate the measured rate \(R(t)\).

figures.label: fig:area-line-parabola
figures.caption: A vertical strip has height \(2x-x^2\), so the area is \(\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx\).

figures.label: fig:right-minus-left-sideways-parabolas
figures.caption: A horizontal strip has length \((2-y^2)-y^2\), so we integrate with respect to \(y\).

figures.label: fig:volume-by-slicing-loaf
figures.caption: Volume by slicing: a differential slice of thickness \(\Delta x\) has volume approximately \(A(x)\Delta x\).

figures.label: fig:shell-parabola
figures.caption: A vertical strip rotated around the \(y\)-axis makes a cylindrical shell.

figures.label: fig:shell-1-over-x
figures.caption: The shell height is \(1/x\), so \(x\cdot(1/x)=1\). The shell setup is especially simple.

figures.label: fig:rod-density-center-mass
figures.caption: For \(\lambda(x)=2+x\) on \([0,4]\), more mass lies to the right, so the center of mass is right of the midpoint.

figures.label: fig:triangular-lamina-center-mass
figures.caption: A triangular lamina can be handled by vertical slices. Each slice contributes mass and moment.

figures.label: fig:work-force-area
figures.caption: Work is the accumulated area under a force-versus-position graph.

figures.label: fig:spring-hookes-law
figures.caption: The farther the spring is stretched, the larger the force needed to hold it.

figures.label: fig:lifting-chain
figures.caption: A piece \(y\) units below the roof must be lifted \(y\) units.

figures.label: fig:pumping-rectangular-tank
figures.caption: Each water slice has the same area, but the lower slices must be lifted farther.

figures.label: fig:hydrostatic-rectangular-plate
figures.caption: A horizontal strip has nearly constant pressure because its depth is nearly constant.

figures.label: fig:hydrostatic-triangle
figures.caption: For the triangular plate, the strip width is a linear function of depth.

figures.label: fig:hydrostatic-circular-window
figures.caption: For a symmetric vertical window, the centroid depth gives the total force quickly.

figures.label: fig:average-value-x-squared
figures.caption: The average value is the height of a rectangle with the same area as the region under the graph.

figures.label: fig:triangular-density
figures.caption: For the density \(p(x)=2x\), probability is area under the density curve.

figures.label: fig:standard-normal-density
figures.caption: For a normal density, probabilities are areas under the bell-shaped curve.

figures.label: fig:arc-length-polygonal
figures.caption: A smooth curve is approximated by short straight pieces. Each small length comes from the Pythagorean theorem.

figures.label: fig:surface-area-band
figures.caption: A small arc segment rotated around the \(x\)-axis sweeps out a thin band.

figures.label: fig:sphere-from-semicircle
figures.caption: Rotating the upper semicircle around the \(x\)-axis produces a sphere.

figures.label: fig:sine-arc-length
figures.caption: Even a simple curve can lead to a length integral with no elementary antiderivative.

figures.label: fig:one-region-several-questions
figures.caption: The same region can produce different integrals depending on what quantity is being measured.

figures.label: fig:trig-substitution-triangles
figures.caption: The three substitutions are right-triangle substitutions. The triangle helps us return to \(x\).

figures.label: fig:integration-decision-tree
figures.caption: A practical order of questions. The arrows are not laws; they are a way to begin thinking.

figures.label: fig:one-over-x-vs-one-over-x-squared
figures.caption: Both curves approach \(0\), but the tail of \(1/x\) has infinite area while the tail of \(1/x^2\) has finite area.

figures.label: fig:infinite-discontinuity-comparison
figures.caption: A function may become infinite near an endpoint and still have finite area. The rate of blowup matters.

figures.label: fig:principal-value-one-over-x
figures.caption: The positive and negative pieces of \(1/x\) cancel symmetrically, but each piece has infinite size.

figures.label: fig:trig-substitution-domain-branches
figures.caption: The expression \(\sqrt{x^2-4}\) has two real branches of the domain. A trigonometric substitution must respect the branch.

figures.label: fig:chapter-11-integration-map
figures.caption: A practical order of questions for integration. The order is flexible, but the first step is always to read the integrand.

figures.label: fig:gaussian-integral-piece
figures.caption: The area \(\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\) exists, even though the antiderivative is not elementary.

figures.label: fig:midpoint-single-interval
figures.caption: The midpoint rule uses one rectangle whose height is taken at the midpoint.

figures.label: fig:trapezoid-single-interval
figures.caption: The trapezoidal rule replaces the graph by the secant line over the interval.

figures.label: fig:composite-midpoint-exp
figures.caption: The composite midpoint rule adds midpoint rectangles over smaller subintervals.

figures.label: fig:trapezoid-concavity-error
figures.caption: For concave-up graphs, trapezoids lie above the curve. For concave-down graphs, trapezoids lie below.

figures.label: fig:simpson-quadratic-through-three-points
figures.caption: Simpson's Rule replaces the graph on two subintervals by the parabola through three sample points.

figures.label: fig:finite-difference-secants
figures.caption: Forward, backward, and centered differences approximate the tangent slope using nearby secant slopes.

figures.label: fig:centered-difference-absolute-value
figures.caption: For \(f(x)=|x|\), the centered difference at \(0\) equals \(0\), but the derivative at \(0\) does not exist.

figures.label: fig:newton-double-root
figures.caption: At a double root, the graph is tangent to the \(x\)-axis. Newton's method still moves toward the root, but much more slowly.

figures.label: fig:newton-map-x2-plus-1
figures.caption: Newton's method for \(x^2+1=0\) over the real numbers produces the iteration \(N(x)=\frac12(x-1/x)\). There is no real root to attract the iterates.

figures.label: fig:normal-density-probability
figures.caption: For a probability density, area under the curve is probability.

figures.label: fig:smooth-vs-rough-integration
figures.caption: High-order numerical rules are most powerful when the function is smooth enough for their error theory.

figures.label: fig:initial-values-select-solutions
figures.caption: The equation \(y'=1-y\) gives a family of solution curves. An initial condition selects one curve.

figures.label: fig:direction-field-one-minus-y
figures.caption: A direction field draws the slope prescribed by \(y'=1-y\) at many points. Solution curves follow the field.

figures.label: fig:logistic-phase-line
figures.caption: For \(y'=y(1-y)\), the arrows show whether solutions move up or down.

figures.label: fig:euler-y-prime-one-minus-y
figures.caption: Euler's method follows the slope field by taking one tangent-line step at a time.

figures.label: fig:cooling-separable
figures.caption: Newton's law of cooling gives exponential approach to the surrounding temperature.

figures.label: fig:logistic-solutions-ch13
figures.caption: Logistic solutions move toward the carrying capacity. From below they rise toward \(K\); from above they fall toward \(K\).

figures.label: fig:logistic-phase-line-ch13
figures.caption: The logistic phase line shows how the equation pushes solutions along the \(P\)-axis.

figures.label: fig:threshold-phase-line
figures.caption: In a threshold model, the population must start above \(A\) to move toward the carrying capacity \(K\).

figures.label: fig:harvesting-growth-curve
figures.caption: A constant harvest is sustainable only if the harvest line meets the natural growth curve.

figures.label: fig:linear-mixing-salt
figures.caption: With a constant incoming concentration, the salt amount approaches an equilibrium.

figures.label: fig:simple-harmonic-motion-cos
figures.caption: Simple harmonic motion oscillates around the equilibrium \(y=0\).

figures.label: fig:damped-oscillation
figures.caption: Damping multiplies the oscillation by a decaying envelope.

figures.label: fig:resonance-response
figures.caption: In the undamped model \(y''+\omega^2y=A\cos(\gamma t)\), the response grows large as \(\gamma\) approaches \(\omega\).

figures.label: fig:predator-prey-phase-plane
figures.caption: A predator-prey system is read in the phase plane. The point \((R(t),W(t))\) moves according to the vector \((R',W')\).

figures.label: fig:oscillator-phase-plane
figures.caption: The simple oscillator becomes a first-order system in the position-velocity plane.

figures.label: fig:yprime-y-squared-lost-solution
figures.caption: The separated family \(y=1/(C-t)\) misses the equilibrium solution \(y=0\).

figures.label: fig:euler-large-step-false-behavior
figures.caption: With a large step, Euler's method can invent behavior opposite to the true solution.

figures.label: fig:same-de-different-initial-conditions
figures.caption: The equation \(y'=1-y\) gives a family. The initial condition selects one solution.

figures.label: fig:parametric-unit-circle
figures.caption: The parameter \(t\) tells how the point moves around the circle.

figures.label: fig:parametric-line-segment
figures.caption: The equations \(x=1+3t,\;y=-2+t\) trace a line segment with a direction.

figures.label: fig:sideways-parabola-parametric
figures.caption: The sideways parabola is easy to trace parametrically: \(x=t^2-1,\;y=t\).

figures.label: fig:parametric-slope-sideways-parabola
figures.caption: For \(x=t^2-1,\;y=t\), the slope is \(\dfrac{1}{2t}\) when \(t\neq0\).

figures.label: fig:circle-horizontal-vertical-tangents
figures.caption: On the unit circle, \(y'=0\) gives horizontal tangents and \(x'=0\) gives vertical tangents.

figures.label: fig:parametric-projectile
figures.caption: The equations \(x=80t,\;y=5+60t-16t^2\) give the path and the motion along it.

figures.label: fig:parametric-circle-length
figures.caption: The circle is traced at constant speed \(R\), so its length is \(2\pi R\).

figures.label: fig:sphere-from-parametric-semicircle
figures.caption: The sphere is built from rotating small arc segments of the upper semicircle.

figures.label: fig:parametric-ellipse-area
figures.caption: The counterclockwise parametrization of an ellipse gives the area \(\pi ab\).

figures.label: fig:cycloid-one-arch
figures.caption: A point on a rolling wheel traces a cycloid. The picture is scaled by \(R\).

figures.label: fig:polar-coordinate-point
figures.caption: Polar coordinates describe a point by distance from the origin and angle from the positive \(x\)-axis.

figures.label: fig:circle-and-spiral-polar
figures.caption: A constant radius gives a circle. A radius growing with angle gives a spiral.

figures.label: fig:polar-circle-offset
figures.caption: The polar equation \(r=2\cos\theta\) is the circle \((x-1)^2+y^2=1\).

figures.label: fig:rose-cardioid-polar
figures.caption: Rose curves and limacons are simple in polar coordinates but awkward in Cartesian coordinates.

figures.label: fig:limacon-inner-loop
figures.caption: When \(r=1+2\cos\theta\), negative values of \(r\) create an inner loop.

figures.label: fig:polar-spiral-slope
figures.caption: A polar graph is a parametric curve with \(\theta\) as the parameter.

figures.label: fig:polar-circle-slope
figures.caption: The polar slope formula gives a horizontal tangent at the top of the circle \(r=2\cos\theta\).

figures.label: fig:polar-sector-area
figures.caption: A small angular slice is approximately a sector of area \(\frac12r^2\Delta\theta\).

figures.label: fig:cardioid-area-polar
figures.caption: The cardioid area is found by accumulating small sectors.

figures.label: fig:polar-intersections-origin
figures.caption: The two circles intersect at \((1,1)\) and at the origin. The origin is reached at different polar angles.

figures.label: fig:parabola-focus-directrix
figures.caption: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.

figures.label: fig:ellipse-hyperbola-standard
figures.caption: Ellipses close up because \(0\le e<1\). Hyperbolas open because \(e>1\).

figures.label: fig:polar-parabola-conic
figures.caption: The polar equation \(r=\frac{4}{1+\cos\theta}\) is a parabola with focus at the pole.

figures.label: fig:eccentricity-polar-conics
figures.caption: In polar form, changing \(e\) changes the conic type. The focus is at the pole.

figures.label: fig:ellipse-focus-at-pole
figures.caption: In the polar form of an ellipse, the focus is placed at the pole. The center is not at the pole.

figures.label: fig:complex-number-as-point
figures.caption: The complex number \(a+bi\) is the point \((a,b)\) in the plane.

figures.label: fig:multiply-by-i-rotation
figures.caption: Multiplication by \(i\) rotates the plane by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise.

figures.label: fig:oscillation-complex-exponential
figures.caption: Sine and cosine are projections of circular motion. Euler's formula writes that motion as \(e^{i\omega t}\).

figures.label: fig:parametric-pause-smooth-parabola
figures.caption: The parametrization \(x=t^3,\;y=t^6\) pauses at the origin, but the geometric curve is the smooth parabola \(y=x^2\).

figures.label: fig:polar-circle-traced-twice
figures.caption: Using \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\) for \(r=2\cos\theta\) traces the same circle twice.

figures.label: fig:three-zero-velocity-tangent-outcomes
figures.caption: At \(t=0\), all three parametrizations have \(x'(0)=y'(0)=0\), but their tangents are different.

figures.label: fig:cycloid-animation-project
figures.caption: A cycloid animation should show the rolling circle and the point \(P(t)\) tracing the curve.

figures.label: fig:sequence-points-approach-one
figures.caption: The sequence \(c_n=1-\frac1n\) approaches \(1\) from below.

figures.label: fig:recursive-halfway-to-three
figures.caption: The recursion \(a_{n+1}=(a_n+3)/2\) moves halfway to \(3\) at each step.

figures.label: fig:partial-sums-halves
figures.caption: The partial sums \(S_n=\frac12+\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2^n}\) approach \(1\).

figures.label: fig:harmonic-grouping-blocks
figures.caption: Grouping the harmonic series into doubled blocks shows that the partial sums keep gaining at least \(1/2\).

figures.label: fig:integral-test-rectangles
figures.caption: For a positive decreasing function, rectangle sums and improper integrals control each other.

figures.label: fig:alternating-harmonic-partial-sums
figures.caption: The alternating harmonic partial sums bounce above and below their limiting value.

figures.label: fig:riemann-rearrangement-idea
figures.caption: The Riemann rearrangement idea: alternate above and below a target, with shrinking overshoots.

figures.label: fig:radius-of-convergence
figures.caption: A power series has a center \(a\) and a radius of convergence \(R\). Endpoint behavior is not decided by the radius alone.

figures.label: fig:safe-interval-inside-radius
figures.caption: Inside a smaller interval \([a-r,a+r]\), a power series is controlled uniformly by geometric bounds.

figures.label: fig:geometric-partial-sums-function
figures.caption: Partial sums of the geometric series approach \(\frac1{1-x}\) on \((-1,1)\).

figures.label: fig:taylor-polynomials-exp
figures.caption: Taylor polynomials for \(e^x\) match more derivatives at the center \(0\).

figures.label: fig:taylor-remainder-gap
figures.caption: The remainder is the vertical gap between the function and its Taylor polynomial at the chosen input.

figures.label: fig:sin-taylor-polynomials
figures.caption: Taylor polynomials for \(\sin x\) are best near the center \(0\), then improve outward as more terms are added.

figures.label: fig:gaussian-taylor-approx
figures.caption: On \([0,1]\), a Taylor polynomial gives a close approximation to \(e^{-x^2}\), and integrating the polynomial gives an approximation to the area.

figures.label: fig:pointwise-xn
figures.caption: The functions \(x^n\) converge pointwise on \([0,1]\), but the convergence is slow near \(x=1\).

figures.label: fig:flat-function
figures.caption: The function \(e^{-1/x^2}\), with \(f(0)=0\), is positive away from \(0\) but is infinitely flat at \(0\).

figures.label: fig:local-series-radius-block
figures.caption: The Maclaurin series for \(\frac1{1-x}\) has radius \(1\). It cannot pass the singularity at \(x=1\), even though the function is defined again at \(x=2\).

figures.label: fig:euler-formula-hook
figures.caption: The Taylor series hint that \(e^{i\theta}\) traces the unit circle.

figures.label: fig:complex-plane-3-plus-4i
figures.caption: The complex number \(3+4i\) is drawn as the point \((3,4)\) in the complex plane.

figures.label: fig:complex-polar-form
figures.caption: Polar form records a complex number by its length \(r\) and angle \(\theta\).

figures.label: fig:multiply-by-i-rotation
figures.caption: Multiplication by \(i\) rotates a complex number counterclockwise by \(90^\circ\).

figures.label: fig:fourth-roots-unity
figures.caption: The equation \(z^4=1\) has four solutions on the unit circle.

figures.label: fig:eit-position-velocity
figures.caption: The position \(e^{it}\) lies on the unit circle. Its velocity \(ie^{it}\) is a quarter-turn of the position.

figures.label: fig:spring-mass-equation
figures.caption: A spring pulls back toward equilibrium. Newton's law turns this restoring force into a second-order equation.

figures.label: fig:spring-solution-amplitude-phase
figures.caption: The solution of \(y''+9y=0\) is periodic. Its amplitude is determined by the initial position and velocity.

figures.label: fig:phase-plane-energy-ellipse
figures.caption: For an undamped oscillator, the phase point \((y,y')\) moves around a closed energy curve.

figures.label: fig:chapter17-damped-oscillation
figures.caption: A lightly damped oscillator still oscillates, but its amplitude shrinks exponentially.

figures.label: fig:damped-forced-response
figures.caption: With damping, resonance produces a large response near the natural frequency, but the amplitude remains finite.

figures.label: fig:fourier-wave-mixture
figures.caption: Adding a few sine and cosine waves already creates a more complicated periodic shape.

figures.label: fig:orthogonality-product-signed-area
figures.caption: The product \(\sin t\sin(2t)\) has signed area zero over \([-\pi,\pi]\).

figures.label: fig:square-wave-fourier-partial-sums
figures.caption: Fourier partial sums approximate a square wave by adding sine waves. Near each jump, ripples remain.

figures.label: fig:oriented-interval-boundary
figures.caption: The boundary of an oriented interval is its ending point minus its starting point.

figures.label: fig:boundary-cancellation
figures.caption: Splitting an interval creates an artificial boundary at \(c\), but the two signs at \(c\) cancel.

figures.label: fig:density-flux-on-line
figures.caption: In one dimension, an interval has two boundary points. Flux through those boundary points changes what is inside.

figures.label: fig:flux-derivative-divergence-1d
figures.caption: When \(q\) increases with \(x\), the outgoing flux from a small interval exceeds the incoming flux.

figures.label: fig:path-variation
figures.caption: To optimize a path, we compare it with nearby paths that keep the endpoints fixed.

figures.label: fig:brachistochrone-cycloid
figures.caption: The brachistochrone is not the shortest path. It is the path of shortest time.

figures.label: fig:final-project-map
figures.caption: Calculus is one connected language: change, accumulation, approximation, models, and boundary terms.
